result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch05-stochastic-differential-equations status: complete --- # Stochastic differential equations A jump process resolves every infection and recovery. A stochastic differential equation (SDE) instead describes continuous-valued fluctuations around a drift. This is useful when the population is large enough for a diffusion approximation to be reasonable, and when we want to connect stochastic simulation with the calculus and solvers used for ODEs. ## Learning goals You will: - derive the chemical Langevin approximation from SIR reaction propensities; - distinguish drift, diffusion columns, and independent Wiener processes; - solve a non-diagonal-noise SDE with the current StochasticDiffEq API; and - diagnose conservation and the possibility of negative populations. ## Model assumptions and classification The baseline is the closed, homogeneously mixing SIR population \((S,I,R)=(990,10,0)\) with \(N=1000\), \(c=10.0\), \(\beta=0.05\), and \(\gamma=0.25\). We retain the two transitions \(S+I\to 2I\) and \(I\to R\), but replace integer event counts by a diffusion. This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population-level** model. “Continuous state” means the numerical approximation can produce real values, not that people are fractional. It is an approximation to the discrete-state CTMC from Chapter 4, and is most defensible when propensities are large and the process is away from absorbing boundaries. ## Equations Write the stoichiometric columns and propensities as $$ V = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -1\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a(X)= \begin{pmatrix} \kappa SI\\ \gamma I \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \kappa=\frac{\beta c}{N}. $$ For a short interval \(dt\), a Poisson event count with mean \(a_jdt\) can be approximated by \[ \operatorname{Poisson}(a_jdt)\approx a_jdt+\sqrt{a_j}\,dW_j, \] where \(dW_j\) are independent Brownian increments with variance \(dt\). Substituting both reactions into the time-change equation gives the chemical Langevin equation $$ dX = V a(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a(X)})\,dW. $$ {#eq-chemical-langevin} Thus the drift \(f(X)=Va(X)\) is \[ f(X)=(-a_1,\ a_1-a_2,\ a_2)^\mathsf{T}, \] and the \(3\times2\) diffusion matrix \(G(X)\) has columns \[ G_{\cdot1}=(-\sqrt{a_1},\sqrt{a_1},0)^\mathsf{T},\qquad G_{\cdot2}=(0,-\sqrt{a_2},\sqrt{a_2})^\mathsf{T}. \] Because each column of \(V\) sums to zero, both the drift and every Brownian increment conserve \(S+I+R\) algebraically. Numerical integration can still accumulate roundoff error. ## Julia implementation `SDEProblem` accepts an in-place drift `f!` and diffusion `g!`. A vector-valued state with a \(3\times2\) diffusion requires `noise_rate_prototype=zeros(3, 2)`: two columns correspond to the two independent Wiener processes. `LambaEM()` is the StochasticDiffEq method for Euler--Maruyama with general (non-diagonal) noise in the installed 7.1.1 environment. The unusual spelling is part of the package API. ::: {#cell-code-ch05-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using OrdinaryDiffEq using StochasticDiffEq using StableRNGs const N = 1000.0 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const κ = β * c / N const u₀ = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] const tspan = (0.0, 30.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.1:30.0) function propensities(u, p) κ, γ = p S, I = max(u[1], 0.0), max(u[2], 0.0) return (κ * S * I, γ * I) end ``` ::: {#code-ch05-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` propensities (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: The `max` operations make the code well-defined if an Euler step crosses a boundary. They do not repair the interpretation of a negative state; the boundary issue is discussed below. ::: {#cell-code-ch05-kernel .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t) infection, recovery = propensities(u, p) du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - recovery du[3] = recovery return nothing end function sir_diffusion!(G, u, p, t) infection, recovery = propensities(u, p) infection_noise = sqrt(infection) recovery_noise = sqrt(recovery) G[1, 1] = -infection_noise G[2, 1] = infection_noise G[3, 1] = 0.0 G[1, 2] = 0.0 G[2, 2] = -recovery_noise G[3, 2] = recovery_noise return nothing end noise_shape = zeros(3, 2) sde_problem = SDEProblem( sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u₀, tspan, (κ, γ); noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape, ) sde_solution = solve( sde_problem, LambaEM(); dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = times, rng = StableRNG(20250711), ) sde_states = Array(sde_solution) ``` ::: {#code-ch05-kernel .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×301 Matrix{Float64}: 990.0 989.411 989.623 988.439 … 182.568 183.329 183.136 10.0 9.86467 10.446 11.4065 23.2206 21.7437 20.9243 0.0 0.723904 -0.0688276 0.15447 794.212 794.927 795.939 ``` ::: ::: The function `sir_diffusion!` is a direct transcription of the two columns of \(G\) in Equation @eq-chemical-langevin. It is intentionally not replaced by independent noise on \(S\), \(I\), and \(R\): doing that would break the reaction-level correlation and population conservation. For a baseline comparison, solve the drift alone: ::: {#cell-code-ch05-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ode_problem = ODEProblem(sir_drift!, u₀, tspan, (κ, γ)) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = times) ode_states = Array(ode_solution) mass_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(sde_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) minimum_state = minimum(sde_states) @assert mass_error < 1e-8 (; mass_error, minimum_state) ``` ::: {#code-ch05-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (mass_error = 2.7284841053187847e-12, minimum_state = -0.06882763332898889) ``` ::: ::: The ODE is not the expected trajectory of every SDE path, but it is the large-population drift comparison. The conservation assertion is stronger: it checks a structural property of the implementation independently of the random realization. ::: {#cell-fig-ch05-diffusion .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (760, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people", title = "Chemical Langevin SIR") for (j, (name, color)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"], [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen])) lines!(ax, times, sde_states[j, :]; color, linewidth = 2, label = "$name (SDE)") lines!(ax, times, ode_states[j, :]; color, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)") end axislegend(ax, position = :rt, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch05-diffusion .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A chemical-Langevin SIR path compared with the deterministic drift. ::: ::: ## Validation The noise columns sum to zero, so conservation is a useful first test. We can also check the diffusion construction directly at one valid state: ::: {#code-ch05-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} G = zeros(3, 2) sir_diffusion!(G, [900.0, 80.0, 20.0], (κ, γ), 0.0) @assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(G; dims = 1)))) < 1e-12 @assert mass_error < 1e-8 ``` ::: At \(N=1000\), the path should broadly follow the ODE while showing realization-to-realization variation. A practical extension is to solve the same `sde_problem` repeatedly with different `StableRNG` seeds and compare the sample mean and standard deviation at the epidemic peak. Such an ensemble comparison tests the approximation statistically; it does not make the diffusion exact. ## Interpretation and limitations The chemical Langevin equation is derived by replacing Poisson reaction counts with Gaussian increments. It is therefore fast and differentiable in much of the interior of the state space, but it can produce \(S<0\), \(I<0\), or \(R<0\), especially near extinction, with large time steps, or in small populations. Clipping a trajectory after each step changes its probability law; it is a pragmatic visualization safeguard, not a principled boundary condition. Alternatives include the exact CTMC, nonnegative tau-leaping, reflecting/absorbing boundary schemes, or transforming the model. `noise_rate_prototype` is an API-level detail with mathematical meaning: leaving it out would ask for diagonal noise, not the two reaction noises in Equation @eq-chemical-langevin. The [StochasticDiffEq SDE tutorial](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/tutorials/sde_example/) documents `SDEProblem`, `EM`, and non-diagonal noise. The approximation itself is the chemical Langevin construction associated with reaction networks [@gillespie1977]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch05-ex1} Run the SDE with `dt` values \(0.1\), \(0.05\), and \(0.01\), using the same seed and `adaptive=false`. For each run, record the maximum conservation error and the minimum state value. Explain why decreasing `dt` usually reduces discretization error but cannot guarantee nonnegative populations for a Gaussian diffusion. ### Exercise 2 {#ch05-ex2} Construct a diagonal-noise SDE that adds independent noise to \(S\), \(I\), and \(R\), keeping the same drift. Compare its conservation error and infected trajectory with the reaction-level model. Identify the precise covariance term that is lost when the two reaction channels are replaced by three independent state noises. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.jl)
